svg.text: Distributed ECU Car — Full Electrical Schematic
Every component, every terminal, every wire. Five blocks; cross-block wires are labelled at both ends. Architecture on SCHEMA_SIGNALS.svg, rails on SCHEMA_POWER.svg
FRDM-MCXA153 + HW-123 + the two level dividers
GND · or J3-14, both are GND
module silkscreen · XDA, XCL, INT stay unconnected
J2-2 means connector J2, pin 2. J1–J4 are the Arduino-form
headers and are two-row, so count carefully — UM12012
Figures 11–12 show the numbering. The silkscreen name is
the quickest check: J2-2 is the pin marked D8 on the board.
P1_8 / P1_9 are the Arduino header's I²C pins, but here they
are LPUART1. The real I²C is P3_27 / P3_28 on mikroBUS.
THE TWO DIVIDERS — build both, one per Arduino
J3-16 (VIN) DOES NOTHING: J22 not populated, path to SYS_5V0 disabled (UM12012).
The pack reaches the MCX only through the buck module, 5.0 V into J3-10. Never with USB in.
On the pack alone you lose VCOM: no console, no FreeMASTER, no debugger.
this pair also runs to ESP32 — block B
P3_27 on mikroBUS · shared with the ESP32
P3_28 on mikroBUS · shared with the ESP32
the pin marked 3V3 · 3.3 V ONLY, never 5 V
with every other ground in the car
this is what sets the address to 0x68
XDA, XCL and INT stay unconnected.
ESP32 · WiFi access point and the laptop link
9 V on VIN is only safe if the board carries an AMS1117 — the
fat 4-pin SOT-223 next to the USB socket, rated to 15 V in.
Some cheaper DevKits fit a tiny 5-pin SOT-23 instead (ME6211,
RT9013). Those stop at about 6 V and 9 V destroys them.
Look before you connect the pack.
AND POINT A FAN AT IT
An AMS1117 dropping 9 V to 3.3 V burns 0.68 W at the ESP32's
WiFi average — about +68 °C in still air, the hot end of
survivable. Moving air roughly halves it, to +31 °C.
The 5 V fan in block E is aimed here for that reason.
A divider sets voltage by ratio, and the ratio only holds while
nothing draws from it. To hold 6 V at 100 mA it needs ~5 Ω
source resistance: 400 mA burnt continuously, 3.6 W in two
resistors — and a 500 mA WiFi burst still drags it to 3.5 V
and resets the board. There is no divider that works here.
Four 1N4001 in series WOULD drop it neatly to ~6.2 V if you
ever buy some — a diode drop barely moves with current.
Four wires. This node has no sensors and no display: it is the
route between the laptop and the VCU, and nothing else.
It is a GATEWAY, not a controller. Everything from the laptop
arrives at the VCU as a request; the VCU decides what to act on.
That is what stops a dropped WiFi link being a safety problem —
and it is what makes the fault-injection demo worth watching.
Roughly 30 GPIO are unused here — by a wide margin the emptiest
board in the project. GPIO6–11 are the flash, 34–39 are input
only, and 0, 2, 5, 12, 15 are strapping pins to leave alone.
Arduino 1 + two fixed HC-SR04P, PIR, buzzer
ECHO is 5 V — never to the MCX
Everything on this node runs from the Arduino 5 V pin now.
Nothing here touches the traction pack — the servos are gone.
D0/D1 free · D2/D3 held for encoders · D13, A3–A5 spare
the screen is blank or all
1602A: RW to GND — write-only. Leave it floating
and the display drives the data bus back at you.
Backlight needs the 220 Ω unless the module already
has one. DB0–DB3 stay unconnected in 4-bit mode.
BASE DRIVE — each PWM pin feeds TWO bases
4 × PN2222A low-side channels · 1N4001 flyback · pack · star ground
STAR GROUND — traction pack −, logic pack −, USB ground, all four board grounds, all four emitters, every component GND
→ BUCK → MCX J3-10 (block A) + ESP32 VIN (block B)
WHY THE FANS ARE NOT DECORATION
A stalled PN2222A dissipates 0.5–1.0 W in a TO-92 rated 0.625 W.
In still air that is about +150 °C of rise; with air moving over it,
nearer +68 °C. The 12 V fan is what turns the drive stage from
marginal into comfortable, so mount it where it sees all four.
The 5 V fan lets the ESP32 take 9 V on VIN without its regulator
A 12 V fan on 9 V turns at roughly 70 %. Quieter, still plenty.
A 5 V fan on 4.8 V is barely slower. Neither is fussy.
Wire both permanently on. Switching an inductive load needs a
flyback diode and there are none spare.
Fan wires carry commutation spikes: run them to the pack
terminals, not through a board's supply, and keep them away
from the UART and I²C runs.
1. Check all four 1N4001 bands point at PACK +. Backwards, each one is a dead short.
2. Motor − goes to a collector, never straight to ground. The transistor is IN the return path.
3. The 10 kΩ pull-downs go base-to-emitter, not base-to-supply.
4. Every ground symbol on this sheet is the same net. Run all four emitters to the star
point in thick wire, and keep signal grounds off that run.
5. ESP32 from the logic pack at VIN, never from an Arduino 3.3 V pin — that gives
30–150 mA and the ESP32 wants 500 in a burst.
6. Both fans run permanently — nothing switches them, so neither needs a flyback
diode. Take both feeds from the pack terminals, not through a board.
7. Only P3_27 / P3_28 are 5 V tolerant on the MCX. Both Arduino TX lines go through the
1 kΩ / 2 kΩ dividers in block A. The two MCX TX lines are plain wire.
8. TX and RX cross: an MCX TX pin always lands on an Arduino D4.
9. The 1602A is a bare HD44780 on six ACT pins in 4-bit mode: RW to ground and a
10 kΩ trimpot on V0. It is the only display on the car.
10. Three supplies is fine. One shared ground is mandatory — without it the links have no
common zero and nothing works properly.
11. Wheels off the floor until duty 0 and a pulled link have both been seen to stop them.
